title: Why the body needs control systems
content:
Suppose you are walking barefoot and you tread on something sharp. Long before you have had time to think, your leg has already adjusted to take the weight off that foot. A moment later you feel the pain, look down and decide what to do about it. Two different control systems produced those two different responses: a fast, automatic one and a slower, considered one. This chapter is about both systems — the nervous system, which sends messages along nerves, and the hormonal system (also called the endocrine system), which sends chemical messages through the blood.

What you already know

In lesson 1.1 you learned that the body is built from cells adapted for particular jobs, and that a muscle cell works by contracting. In lesson 1.2 you learned that enzymes work best within a narrow range of conditions, including body temperature. Those facts explain why control matters: if the body could not detect changes and respond to them quickly, muscles could not be ordered to contract at the right moment, and the conditions enzymes need would drift away from the range they work in.

The words that describe every response

Scientists use five words to describe any response, whatever the control system:

  • a stimulus is a change in the environment (or inside the body) — the sharp object under your foot, or light suddenly shining in your eye;
  • a receptor is a cell or part of the body that detects the stimulus;
  • a co-ordinator processes the information and decides on a response — the brain, the spinal cord, or (for hormones) a gland such as the pancreas;
  • an effector carries out the response — a muscle that contracts, or a gland that releases a substance;
  • a response is the resulting action — pulling your foot away, or your pupil narrowing.

Every example in this chapter fits the same chain:

The key idea of this chapter: stimulus → receptor → co-ordinator → effector → response. Nervous responses pass along this chain as fast electrical impulses; hormonal responses pass along it as chemicals carried in the blood. Keep the chain in mind and every new term in this chapter will have an obvious place in it.

Where we are going

The next five pages build up the nervous system: the central nervous system, the cells that carry its messages, the junctions between those cells, and the reflex arc that produces automatic responses. Then we apply the same ideas to two responses of the eye, the pupil reflex and focusing. The last five pages move to the hormonal system: glands, hormones, the control of blood glucose by insulin, and what happens when that control fails — diabetes. The chapter closes with a practical on measuring reaction time.

title: The central nervous system
content:
The nervous system has two main divisions. The central nervous system (CNS) is made of the brain and the spinal cord. Everything else — the nerves running to your fingers, your skin, your eyes and your muscles — makes up the peripheral nervous system, the network that connects the CNS to the rest of the body.

What the brain and spinal cord do

The brain is the body’s main co-ordinator. It receives information arriving along nerves from receptors all over the body, compares it with what the body needs, and sends instructions out along nerves to effectors. Conscious decisions are made in the brain: choosing to pick up a pen, or to step around an obstacle.

The spinal cord is a thick bundle of nerve tissue that runs from the brain down inside the backbone (the vertebrae, which protect it, just as the skull protects the brain). It has two jobs. First, it carries messages between the brain and the body — a nerve message from your foot travels up the spinal cord to reach the brain, and the brain’s instruction travels back down it. Second, it is itself a co-ordinator for rapid, automatic responses: reflexes, which you will meet on page 5, are processed in the spinal cord without waiting for the brain.

Why the arrangement matters

Because all long-distance nerve traffic passes through the spinal cord, damage to it cuts off the lines of communication below the injury. A person with a severed spinal cord may still have working muscles and working receptors below that point, but the messages can no longer reach the co-ordinator, so those body parts cannot respond to instructions from the brain.

Practice

Name the two organs of the central nervous system, and state one job of the spinal cord that the brain itself cannot do.

Show the answer

The brain and the spinal cord. The spinal cord co-ordinates reflexes by itself — it processes certain incoming messages and sends out a response without the brain being involved in the decision. (Acceptable alternatives: acting as the route for messages between the brain and the body is a job the spinal cord does that the brain cannot do alone, because the brain has no direct connection to the nerves of the limbs.)

title: Neurones: the cells that carry messages
content:
The cells that carry messages in the nervous system are called neurones (sometimes written neurons). A neurone is adapted to carry an electrical impulse, a tiny wave of electrical change, quickly along its length. The impulse always travels in one direction through the cell.

The main parts to know are the dendrites, short branching fibres that receive messages from other cells; the cell body, which contains the nucleus; and the axon (the long fibre labelled in the diagram), which carries the impulse towards the nerve endings. Some axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating sheath, which speeds the impulse along.

Three kinds of neurone, three directions

Neurones are classified by the direction of the message they carry:

  • sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors towards the central nervous system;
  • relay neurones (also called connector neurones) lie inside the CNS and pass the message between other neurones;
  • motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS out to effectors — muscles or glands.

A common misconception: a neurone and a nerve are not the same thing. A single neurone is one cell. A nerve is a bundle of many neurones wrapped together — like a cable made of many wires. When you read “a message travels along a nerve”, it is really travelling along one of the many neurones inside that nerve.

Practice

A pain receptor in a person’s hand detects a hot surface. Name the type of neurone that carries this message to the spinal cord, and name the type that would carry an instruction from the spinal cord to a muscle in the arm.

Show the answer

A sensory neurone carries the message from the receptor to the CNS, and a motor neurone carries the instruction from the CNS to the muscle (the effector). A relay neurone may connect the two inside the spinal cord, but the sensory and motor neurones are the ones crossing the distances named in the question.

title: The synapse: crossing the gap
content:
Neurones do not touch each other. Where the end of one neurone comes close to the start of the next there is a tiny gap called a synapse. The electrical impulse cannot jump across a gap, so the message has to be converted into a chemical form to get across.

How the message crosses

The sequence has four stages:

  1. The electrical impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone.
  2. The neurone releases a chemical messenger (a neurotransmitter) into the gap.
  3. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap — it spreads from where it is concentrated to where there is less of it.
  4. It binds to receptor molecules on the membrane of the next neurone, which triggers a new electrical impulse in that neurone.

Notice how well this matches what you know about diffusion from lesson 1.1: the neurotransmitter moves down its concentration gradient, from the crowded side of the gap to the empty side.

Why the synapse is designed this way

The receptors for the neurotransmitter sit only on the far side of the gap, never on the near side. That gives the message a built-in direction: impulses can cross from the first neurone to the second, but never backwards. Synapses also let one neurone connect to many others, so the CNS can route a single incoming message to several different places at once — for example, to the brain (so you feel what happened) and to a motor neurone (so you can react).

A common misconception: the electrical impulse does not “leak” across the gap. Nothing electrical crosses a synapse. The electrical message is converted to a chemical message at the gap and back into an electrical message on the other side.

Practice

Explain why a nerve message can travel across a synapse in only one direction.

Show the answer

Only the first neurone releases the neurotransmitter, and only the second neurone has receptors that can detect it. Because the receptor molecules are found only on the far side of the gap, the message can be passed onwards but can never be sent back the way it came, so transmission through the synapse is one-way.

title: Reflex actions and the reflex arc
content:
A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus. It does not involve the conscious part of the brain: the message is processed in the spinal cord, and the response happens before you are aware of it. Blinking when something moves towards your eye, coughing when food goes down the wrong way, and pulling your hand away from a hot surface are all reflexes.

The pathway the message follows is called the reflex arc. The diagram shows the classic example: a hand touching something hot.

The route, step by step

  1. Stimulus: the hot object changes the temperature of the skin.
  2. Receptor: a pain receptor in the skin detects the change and starts an impulse.
  3. Sensory neurone: carries the impulse to the spinal cord.
  4. Relay neurone: inside the spinal cord, passes the message straight to a motor neurone. (A second message also travels on to the brain — that is why you feel the pain shortly afterwards.)
  5. Motor neurone: carries the impulse to the muscle in the arm.
  6. Response: the muscle contracts and pulls the hand away.

Why the detour past the brain is a design advantage

It might seem like a weakness that the brain is left out of the decision. It is the opposite. Sending the message all the way to the brain, having it weigh up options and send a decision back, would take longer — precious time during which the hand stays on the hot surface. By processing the response in the spinal cord, the body protects itself as fast as its nerves can carry messages. Reflexes are the body’s fast lane.

Worked example: putting the arc in order

The question. A student writes the parts of the reflex arc in this order: muscle contracts, motor neurone, receptor in skin, sensory neurone, relay neurone. Reorder the five parts correctly, starting from the stimulus.

Step 1. Find the start of the chain: the stimulus must be detected before anything else can happen, so the receptor comes first.

Step 2. From the receptor, the message always moves towards the CNS, so the sensory neurone is second, and the relay neurone (inside the CNS) is third.

Step 3. From the CNS the message moves outwards: the motor neurone is fourth, and the response — the muscle contracting — is last.

The correct order is therefore: receptor in skin → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → muscle contracts. (In CCEA examinations, ordering questions like this commonly award marks for any two steps in the correct sequence, so checking the order of every pair of steps is worth the time.)

Practice

Your knee is tapped just below the kneecap and your lower leg swings forward. Explain why this response happens without you deciding to move your leg.

Show the answer

The tap is a stimulus detected by receptors in the leg. The message travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord, where a relay neurone passes it directly to a motor neurone, which carries it to the leg muscles, making them contract. Because the reflex arc is processed in the spinal cord and does not involve the conscious part of the brain, the movement is automatic — it happens without any decision.
